title: Intro to APIs with the requests library
summary: Talk to web services from Python — send HTTP requests, read JSON responses, and handle errors with the requests library.
objectives: Explain what an API is and why programs use them to share data
Send a GET request to a real API with requests.get
Read the status code and check whether a request succeeded
Parse a JSON response into a Python dictionary with .json()
Pass query parameters and headers to customise a request
Handle errors with raise_for_status and try / except
Keep API keys out of your code using environment variables

quiz.why: An API — Application Programming Interface — is a defined way for one program to request data or actions from another.

quiz.q: Which HTTP status code means the request succeeded?
quiz.why: 200 means OK. 404 means not found, and 500 means a server error.

quiz.q: Which requests method turns a JSON response body into a Python dictionary?
quiz.why: response.json() decodes the JSON body into Python dicts and lists. .text gives the raw string.

quiz.answer: It raises an exception if the response status code indicates an error (4xx or 5xx), so failures aren't silently ignored.
quiz.why: Without it, a failed request still returns a response object and your code may carry on with bad data.

quiz.q: Why should you store an API key in an environment variable instead of writing it in your code?
quiz.answer: So the secret key is not committed to git or shared publicly; it keeps credentials out of source control.
quiz.why: Hard-coded keys leak when code is pushed to a repo; environment variables keep secrets separate from code.

quiz.q: In requests.get(url, params={...}), what does the params argument do?
options: Adds query string parameters to the URL
quiz.why: params builds the query string, e.g. ?q=python&limit=5, and handles encoding for you.

body_markdown:
## What is an API?

An **API** (Application Programming Interface) is a defined way for one program to ask another program for data or actions. When you check the weather in an app, that app sends a request to a weather service's API and gets data back. For an A I engineer, APIs are how you pull in data, call models, and connect systems.

Most web APIs work over **HTTP**, the same protocol your browser uses. You send a **request** to a URL; the server sends back a **response**.

## Installing and importing requests

The `requests` library is the friendliest way to make HTTP calls in Python. Install it once with pip.

```bash
pip install requests
```

Then import it in your script.

```python
import requests
```

## Your first GET request

A **GET** request asks a server for data. We call `requests.get` with a URL and get back a **response object**. The `status_code` tells us how it went — `200` means success.

```python
import requests

url = "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1"
response = requests.get(url)

print(response.status_code)   # 200
print(response.json())        # {'userId': 1, 'id': 1, ...}
```

## Reading JSON responses

Most APIs reply in **JSON**, a text format of keys and values. Calling `.json()` converts it into a Python **dictionary** you can index like any other dict.

```python
data = response.json()
print(data["title"])        # the to-do's title
print(data["completed"])    # True or False
```

## Parameters, headers, and errors

Many APIs accept **query parameters** to filter results, and **headers** for things like authentication. Always check for errors: `raise_for_status()` throws if the request failed, and a `try`/`except` keeps your program from crashing.

```python
import requests

params = {"userId": 1}
try:
    r = requests.get("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos", params=params, timeout=5)
    r.raise_for_status()
    todos = r.json()
    print(len(todos), "to-dos found")
except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
    print("Request failed:", e)
```

## Keeping API keys safe

Paid APIs give you a secret **API key**. Never write it directly in your code — if you push to git, the key leaks. Store it in an **environment variable** and read it with `os.environ`.

```python
import os
import requests

api_key = os.environ["MY_API_KEY"]
headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + api_key}
r = requests.get("https://api.example.com/data", headers=headers)
```

## Your task

Pick a free public API (such as JSONPlaceholder), send a GET request, check the status code, and print one field from the JSON response.

slides.title: Intro to APIs with requests
slides.narration: Welcome back. In this lesson we open the door to the wider internet. You'll learn how to pull data from web services using A P Is and Python's requests library. By the end you'll be able to send a request, read the response, turn it into a Python dictionary, and handle errors gracefully. This is a skill you'll use constantly as an A I engineer.

slides.title: What is an API?
bullets: An A P I lets one program ask another for data.
Most web A P Is work over H T T P.
You send a request; the server sends a response.
It's how apps fetch weather, prices, and more.
slides.narration: So what is an A P I? It stands for Application Programming Interface, and it's simply a defined way for one program to ask another for data or actions. When a weather app shows you the forecast, it asked a weather service's A P I behind the scenes. Most of these work over H T T P, the same protocol your browser uses: you send a request to a U R L, and the server sends a response back.

slides.title: The requests library
bullets: requests is the friendliest way to make H T T P calls.
Install it once with pip.
Then import it in your script.
slides.narration: Python doesn't make web requests beautifully on its own, so we use a library called requests. It's the most popular and friendliest tool for the job. You install it just once using pip, the package installer, by typing pip install requests in your terminal. After that, you bring it into any script with import requests.

slides.title: Your first GET request
bullets: A GET request asks a server for data.
requests.get returns a response object.
status_code of 200 means success.
slides.code:
import requests
url = "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1"
r = requests.get(url)
print(r.status_code)   # 200
slides.narration: Let's make our first call. A GET request is how you ask a server for data. We call requests dot get with a U R L, and it hands back a response object. The first thing to check is the status code. Two hundred means everything went fine. Here we're hitting a free test A P I called Jason Placeholder that returns a sample to-do item.

slides.title: Status codes
bullets: 200 means OK — success.
404 means not found.
500 means a server error.
Always check before trusting the data.
slides.narration: Every response comes with a status code, a three-digit number telling you what happened. Two hundred means OK, your request succeeded. Four oh four means not found, perhaps the U R L is wrong. Five hundred means the server itself had a problem. Get into the habit of checking the status code before you trust the data you got back.

slides.title: Reading JSON
bullets: Most A P Is reply in JSON.
JSON is keys and values, like a dictionary.
Call .json() to get a Python dict.
slides.narration: Most A P Is reply in a format called Jason, spelled J S O N, which is just keys and values, very much like a Python dictionary. The requests library makes this easy: call dot json with parentheses on the response, and it converts that text into a real Python dictionary. From there you index it by key, exactly like any dictionary you've used before.

slides.title: Query parameters
bullets: Parameters filter or customise the request.
Pass them as a dictionary to params.
requests builds the U R L for you.
slides.narration: Often you don't want everything an A P I offers, just a slice of it. That's what query parameters are for. You pass them as a dictionary to the params argument, and requests builds the query string on the end of the U R L for you, handling all the tricky encoding. Here we ask only for to-dos belonging to user one.

slides.title: Handling errors
bullets: raise_for_status() throws on a failed request.
Wrap calls in try / except.
Add a timeout so it can't hang forever.
slides.narration: Networks are unreliable, so good code expects failure. The method raise for status throws an error if the response was a four hundred or five hundred, so problems don't slip past silently. Wrap your call in a try and except block to catch those errors and keep your program alive. And always pass a timeout, so a slow server can't make your script hang forever.

slides.title: Keep API keys safe
bullets: Paid A P Is give you a secret key.
Never hard-code it — it leaks on git push.
Store it in an environment variable.
slides.code:
import os
key = os.environ["MY_API_KEY"]
headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + key}
requests.get(url, headers=headers)
slides.narration: Many real A P Is require a secret key to identify you. Here's a rule you must never break: do not write that key directly in your code. If you push to git, the whole world can see it. Instead, store the key in an environment variable on your machine and read it with os dot environ. Then pass it along in the headers, usually as an authorization header.
